Mumbai: The Indian rupee extended its winning streak for the fifth consecutive session on Thursday, while crude oil prices tumbled as investors bet that the Democrats' sweeping gains in the US midterm elections could push President Donald Trump towards an exit from the Iran war.
The rupee opened higher by 29 paise at 94.35 per dollar against Wednesday's close of 94.64.
Meanwhile, Brent crude futures fell $1.16 or per cent to $93.46 a barrel extending the decline for a fourth consecutive session.
Similarly, US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures declined $1.47 or 1.66 per cent to $86.65.
Both benchmarks had tumbled about 10 per cent and settled below $100 per barrel mark in the previous session.
Moreover, crude prices have now fallen nearly 16 per cent so far this week.
The selloff follows the Democrats' victory in both chambers of Congress, dealing a major setback to Trump and his Republican Party.

A Democratic-controlled Congress could constrain the US president's military options and tighten spending on the conflict, giving him a greater incentive to pursue a negotiated exit rather than risk further escalation.
US President Donald Trump also said that Washington had no immediate plans to strike Iran, as per reports.
Apart from that, crude shipments through the Strait of Hormuz -- the key waterway for most Gulf oil supplies -- have recovered to close to pre-war levels, albeit at a higher cost.
The dollar index -- which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies -- fell 0.06 per cent to 101.41 after a 0.36 per cent decline in the prior session.

stories.summary: Washington, Nov 05: US President Donald Trump on Wednesday said it was “largely true” that the war in Iran cost the Republicans heavy losses in the midterm election, but struck a defiant note, saying he would do it again as it was the “only answer” in the “long term”. "Well, I think it's largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit short term," Trump told reporters when asked about Vice President J D Vance’s remarks that the Iran war led to Republican losses in the election. "But at the same time, if I had it to do again, I'd have to do it again. Because long term, it's the only answer. You can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon," he said. The president insisted that the US would have done nothing different as far as the war was concerned. "But I can tell you that as far as that war is concerned, I would have done nothing different. We've totally broken their military. The navy's gone. Their air force is gone. Their anti-aircraft is gone," Trump said. “The Iran thing, we had to do, and we continue to do it. We have tremendous oil flowing out of the Hormuz Strait now. At the beginning, there was none. And, probably that's the primary reason – the price, not the war, the price (of oil),” Trump said. The president also said that he was not considering replacing Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, despite public dissatisfaction with the war with Iran. Hegseth is “doing a great job", he said. Vice President JD Vance, often eyed as Trump's likely successor at the White House, blamed the president's war in Iran for Republicans' midterm wipeout.

article_sentences: Heavy rains triggered by Cyclone Murasu wreaked havoc in Aswaraopet, Dammapeta and several other mandals of Bhadradri Kothagudem district on Wednesday, inundating vast stretches of agricultural land and disrupting vehicular movement on several roads.

According to sources, the temporary ring bund of the Peddavagu medium irrigation project in Aswaraopet mandal reportedly suffered a breach, resulting in the inundation of agricultural fields in nearby villages.
Ponds and streams across the mandal swelled following overnight heavy downpour, causing waterlogging in low-lying areas of Aswaraopet, Naramvarigudem and other places.
Nemalipeta colony in Dammapeta was also inundated with rainwater, causing severe inconvenience to residents.
Vehicular movement on the Palvancha-Dammapeta road came to a standstill after a diversion road near Rajupeta in Mulakalapalli mandal was washed away by floodwaters on Wednesday morning.
Standing paddy and cotton crops, besides harvested produce were reportedly damaged by the heavy rains across several parts of the erstwhile undivided Khammam district, dealing a blow to farmers.
Local holidays were declared for schools in some mandals on Wednesday in view of the heavy rainfall triggered by Cyclone Murasu.

stories.title: US election results could slow AI data-centre investments, support Treasury bonds: Report
stories.summary: Proposed restrictions over electricity consumption, water usage and local infrastructure costs could reshape investment plans across three major US data-centre markets
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence

article_sentences: The US midterm election outcome could put 141 gigawatts (GW) of planned data-centre capacity at greater risk of policy restrictions, potentially slowing artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure investments while supporting US Treasury bonds, according to a report by ICICI Bank.
The report said Democratic victories in the governorships of Texas, Georgia and Ohio have increased the possibility of tighter scrutiny of data-centre projects.
The three states together account for nearly 33 per cent of the country’s operating and planned data-centre capacity.
The incoming governors had campaigned on proposals to pause or restrict new projects, citing concerns over electricity and water consumption, utility costs and the impact on local communities.
The three states have a combined data-centre capacity of 156 GW, of which around 141 GW is still planned and only 15 GW is operational.
Texas alone accounts for 22 per cent of national capacity, while Georgia and Ohio account for 5 per cent and 6 per cent, respectively.
ICICI Bank cautioned that the election outcome does not guarantee the proposed restrictions will be implemented, as policy changes would require legislative and regulatory support.
However, it could lead to a “potential slowdown in further investments into data centres”, rather than a nationwide reversal of the AI investment cycle.

The report also said the outcome could be positive for US Treasury markets as tighter scrutiny of data-centre projects may slow AI capital expenditure and reduce borrowing by large technology companies.
Lower investment spending could also moderate economic growth and inflation pressures, potentially reducing the need for further interest rate increases by the Federal Reserve.
Following the election results, US two-year Treasury yields fell by as much as 9 basis points to 4.54 per cent before recovering to 4.59 per cent.
The 10-year yield declined by 7 basis points to 4.89 per cent before settling at 4.91 per cent.

stories.headline: Failure To Seek Recount During Counting Alone Does Not Justify Rejecting An Election Petition: Chhattisgarh High Court
stories.title: Failure To Seek Recount During Counting Alone Does Not Justify Rejecting An Election Petition: Chhattisgarh High Court
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The Chhattisgarh High Court has upheld an Election Tribunal's decision refusing to reject an election petition merely because the election petitioner had not sought recounting of votes during the counting process.
The Court held that specific allegations of discrepancies in vote tabulation and manipulation of election records raised triable issues which required adjudication on evidence.

Justice Amitendra Kishore Prasad was hearing a writ petition filed by the returned candidate challenging the Election Tribunal's rejection of his application under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, seeking rejection of an election petition.
The election petition had raised a challenge to the election of the petitioner, alleging irregularities in the counting and tabulation of votes at Polling Booth No. 187.

The returned candidate argued that recounting was not sought during the counting process on February 23, 2025, as contemplated under Rule 80(1) read with Rule 80(5) of the Chhattisgarh Panchayat Nirvachan Niyam, 1995.
Relying on Supreme Court decisions, he contended that the election petition was not maintainable in the absence of a request for recounting at the appropriate stage.
The Court noted that while deciding an application under Order VII Rule 11 CPC, the court must examine the election petition as a whole and determine whether its pleadings disclose a cause of action.
The defence raised by the returned candidate and disputed questions requiring evidence cannot ordinarily be considered at this preliminary stage.
The Court observed that the absence of a recounting request during counting did not, by itself, dispense with the requirement of examining the entire election petition.

“The mere fact that no request for recounting was made at the time of counting does not, by itself, dispense with the requirement of examining the entire election petition to determine whether it discloses a cause of action or is ex facie barred by law,” the Court remarked.
The Court further noted that the election petitioner had explained that the discrepancies became apparent only after he obtained the certified tabulation chart.
The Court clarified that it was not deciding whether this explanation was ultimately sufficient or whether the allegations were true; those questions were for the Election Tribunal to determine.

Meanwhile, the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen claimed they fired strikes on an airport in the Saudi capital of Riyadh. The Israeli military said it struck two suspects in Lebanon, killing one person. Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Wednesday. Read our full coverage here. The broader region has been on edge for weeks over whether the US will resume full-scale military operations against Iran. Talks are ongoing aimed at preventing renewed fighting. Underscoring the mutual hostility, thousands marched through Tehran on Wednesday at a government-organized demonstration commemorating the anniversary of the 1979 takeover of the U.S. Embassy. Pro-government demonstrators burned American and Israeli flags and chanted “Death to America” and “Death to Israel.” UN peacekeeping chief says Lebanon needs UN presence and urges a Security Council decision Jean-Pierre Lacroix said Wednesday that Lebanese officials fear a “security vacuum” between Israeli forces and the Lebanese army when the UN peacekeeping mission known as UNIFIL ends December 31. Lacroix, who recently returned from the Middle East, warned of the risks of leaving the two armies “sort of face-to-face” without a third-party presence. He questioned who would monitor the U.N.-drawn Blue Line separating Israel and Lebanon, prevent unintended clashes and support communities in southern Lebanon. The border region patrolled by UNIFIL has experienced decades of violence, including a full-scale war between Israel and Hezbollah militants in 2024. Israel has long accused UNIFIL of failing to prevent Hezbollah from building up its military presence along the border. Lacroix said efforts to disarm Hezbollah had failed because “there was no political will.” The United States, Israel’s closest ally, successfully pushed the U.N. Security Council to end the mission after nearly five decades. U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres proposed three options in June to maintain U.N. monitoring along the border. Lacroix said unarmed UN military observers would still be authorized to operate in southern Lebanon but questioned how they could do so without protection or support. He said a Security Council resolution adopted in 2000 remains in effect. The council is scheduled to discuss it Nov. 19. Houthis claim strikes on targets in Saudi Arabia In Yemen, the Iran-backed Houthis on Wednesday claimed without providing evidence that they targeted King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi Arabian capital of Riyadh as well as several areas in southern parts of the country. Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said rebels fired a ballistic missile toward the airport, causing what he described as “major damages” to the airport. He also claimed that the group fired a drone at a radar installation and a ballistic missile at a command and control center in the Jazan province. The Associated Press couldn’t independently verify these claims. The Saudi information ministry didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. The Saudi civil defense issued an alert in Riyadh overnight and other warning alerts of potential “danger” in Jazan and Najran early Wednesday. The Houthi-run health ministry said in a statement the strike hit a house in the district of Maqbanah and also wounded six other children. The Houthi media aired footage it said was of the struck building. The footage showed a heavily damaged concrete building, with large sections of the roof and walls collapsing. The ministry blamed Saudi Arabia, which didn’t immediately comment on the accusations. It was the latest deadly strike in Yemen since the country’s civil war was revived more than three months ago. The fighting pits the Iranian-backed Houthis against Saudi Arabia and its ally, Yemen's internationally recognized government. Israeli drone strike on southern Lebanon In Lebanon, the Health Ministry said the strike on a motorcycle in the village of Qabrikha killed one person and wounded another. The Israeli military said in a statement that it had “struck two suspects who were observing IDF soldiers” without providing further details. The attack was the first in nearly a month as such drone strikes have been rare since a US-brokered ceasefire in late June ended the latest Israel-Hezbollah war.

stories.headline: Arab parties extend a hand to try and topple Netanyahu, but challenges remain
stories.title: Arab parties extend a hand to try and topple Netanyahu, but challenges remain
stories.summary: Tayibe(Israel), Nov 5: A veteran Arab lawmaker in Israel says his bloc is willing to break with decades of precedent and join forces with Jewish-led parties in a shared bid to end Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's long rule. “We want to do things that we did not do in the past in order to remove this criminal government,” Ahmad Tibi, a senior member of the Arab Joint List, told The Associated Press. But any such partnership could be politically fraught for both sides. For the Joint List, it would mean backing a government unlikely to end Israel's wars or curb settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank. For Netanyahu's opponents, it would mean aligning with parties that not only criticise Israeli policies, but reject its identity as a Jewish state. After historic voter turnout delivered Arab-led parties a record share in Israel's parliament, Tibi said the Joint List is willing to support an anti-Netanyahu government without joining it. That could reassure Jewish-led factions that view them with suspicion and satisfy their own constituents. It would still give the Joint List major influence. Only one Arab party has ever served in an Israeli government, in 2021. But that party, Ra'am, is much more conciliatory than the Joint List and held fewer seats. Ra'am is willing to join another anti-Netanyahu government as a partner, but any such arrangement would still need the support of the Joint List. If the Jewish-led parties reject such a partnership, then it would prove Israel is “an ethnocracy, not an absolute democracy for all citizens,” Tibi said. The Joint List's positions put it at odds with most Israelis. --------------------------------------------------------------- Most of the Palestinian population in what is now Israel fled or were expelled during the 1948 war surrounding its creation. Those who remained were granted citizenship, including the right to vote, and today they and their descendants make up some 20 per cent of the population. Many Jewish Israelis have historically viewed Arab-led political parties with suspicion. That distrust has been reinforced by lawmakers who have defended or praised Israel's enemies. The Joint List, a coalition of three left-wing and nationalist parties, rejects what it refers to as the “racist Zionist consensus” in Israel. It calls for partnering with Jewish Israelis who support a Palestinian state in the West Bank, Gaza and east Jerusalem, territories occupied in the 1967 Mideast war. It rejects Israel's identity as a Jewish state, calling for equal rights for all its citizens. Many Jewish Israelis see that as support for the country's enemies at a time of war. Netanyahu has encouraged such sentiments, lodging unproven accusations of electoral fraud against the Arab-led parties and portraying them as a threat to national security. A dilemma for Netanyahu's opponents --------------------------------------------- That creates a dilemma for Netanyahu's main opponents, led by former general Gadi Eisenkot. In the campaign, they portrayed Netanyahu as a corrupt leader who failed to prevent the October 7, 2023, attack and then blocked a public inquiry into it. They cast the election in existential terms, saying Netanyahu's far-right government threatened Israel's democratic institutions. They won 48 seats in the 120-member Knesset, compared to 53 for Netanyahu's coalition. The Joint List won 11 seats and Ra'am won 8, making them crucial to forming an anti-Netanyahu majority. The Joint List could help an anti-Netanyahu bloc take power by voting for it or by abstaining to lower the threshold needed for a majority. Either arrangement could allow opposition parties to form a government without requiring the Joint List to become part of their administration. Joining could put its lawmakers in the uncomfortable position of being part of a government waging wars in Gaza and Lebanon that they oppose. Some of Eisenkot's allies welcome Arab support while others are opposed, pointing to past statements by Joint List leaders they argue deny Israel's legitimacy or support its enemies. Tibi said he was under no illusions that a partnership with Netanyahu's opponents would end the wars or bring about a Palestinian state. But he said a “repair government” would improve the lives of Palestinian citizens, by ending Netanyahu's rule and also potentially addressing local issues like a wave of violent crime in Arab communities. It's unclear what conditions would be required -------------------------------------------------- Eisenkot has said Arab-led parties must meet certain conditions in any partnership, including calling Hamas a terrorist group that needs to be destroyed. Tibi said the conditions do not apply to parties like the Joint List that want to provide outside support. The Joint List and Ra'am have denounced Hamas' October 7, 2023, attack and any violence against civilians. But they have refused to brand Hamas a terrorist group or call for its destruction, saying that doing so would justify Israel's devastating military campaign in Gaza. Tibi said both the October 7 attack and Israel's response to it were immoral. The veteran lawmaker has long been a lightning rod for right-wing attacks on Arab parties. During Israel's 2019 elections, Netanyahu, popularly known as Bibi, campaigned on the slogan “Bibi or Tibi?” to warn voters that opposing him meant relying on Arab-led parties to form a government. Tibi said Tuesday that the election result had turned the slogan on its head. “When he said Bibi or Tibi,' he incited against Arabs,” he said. “Now, it's Tibi,' because Arab voters went in a very massive way to take part in the elections. It's definitely our story this time.”

stories.summary: Shares of commercial vehicle majors Ashok Leyland and Tata Motors rallied as much as 12% on Thursday after a sharp drop in oil prices, which boosted investor sentiment amid hopes of an Iran deal.In today’s session, Ashok Leyland shares rallied as much as 12% to Rs 172 on the BSE, while commercial vehicle major Tata Motors jumped 9% to Rs 440.Why are these 2 stocks rising?1.) Oil tumbles 10% in two days - Crude oil prices crashed over a percent on Thursday, extending losses from a 9% plunge in the previous session as markets assessed the implications of the Democrats' sweeping victory over Republicans in the US midterm elections.The political setback raised expectations that mounting pressure on the Republican Party could push the Trump administration toward ending the war with Iran through a negotiated settlement.Brent crude was trading at $93.51 a barrel, down more than 1%, or $1.05 in absolute terms. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude slipped 1.35% to below $87 a barrel. In the previous session, Brent futures settled $8.98, or 8.7%, lower at $94.62 a barrel, while WTI crude futures dropped $7.97, or 8.3%, to $88.12. Both benchmarks ended Wednesday at their lowest levels since August 31.Falling crude oil prices are positive for commercial vehicle (CV) manufacturers such as Ashok Leyland and Tata Motors as diesel accounts for a significant portion of fleet operators' running costs. Lower fuel prices improve the operating economics of truck and bus owners, potentially encouraging fleet expansion, replacement demand and fresh vehicle purchases. Cheaper crude also reduces input and logistics costs for automakers, supporting margins. Additionally, lower fuel prices can ease inflationary pressures and improve overall economic activity, benefiting freight movement and transportation demand.2.) Buoyant market mood - The Indian stock market opened Thursday's session on a strong note, with benchmark indices Sensex and Nifty rallying nearly 2% amid a favourable mix of global and domestic cues. Gains by Democrats in the US midterm elections, marking a setback for US President Donald Trump, along with easing crude oil prices, boosted investor sentiment and extended Dalal Street's recovery rally for a second consecutive session.The Sensex surged over 1,400 points to cross the 78,700 mark, while the Nifty 50 jumped more than 400 points to reclaim 24,350. The sharp rally added nearly Rs 8 lakh crore to the combined market capitalisation of BSE-listed companies, taking it to Rs 501 lakh crore.Broader markets also participated in the rally, with the Nifty Midcap 100 and Nifty Smallcap 250 indices gaining up to 1.5%. stories.summary: Mumbai, Nov 5 : The Indian rupee extended its winning streak for the fifth consecutive session on Thursday, while crude oil prices tumbled as investors bet that the Democrats' sweeping gains in the US midterm elections could push President Donald Trump towards an exit from the Iran war. The rupee opened higher by 29 paise at 94.35 per dollar against Wednesday's close of 94.64. Meanwhile, Brent crude futures fell $1.16 or per cent to $93.46 a barrel extending the decline for a fourth consecutive session. Similarly, US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures declined $1.47 or 1.66 per cent to $86.65. Both benchmarks had tumbled about 10 per cent and settled below $100 per barrel mark in the previous session. Moreover, crude prices have now fallen nearly 16 per cent so far this week. The selloff follows the Democrats' victory in both chambers of Congress, dealing a major setback to Trump and his Republican Party. A Democratic-controlled Congress could constrain the US president's military options and tighten spending on the conflict, giving him a greater incentive to pursue a negotiated exit rather than risk further escalation. Reports claim that a full-scale assault on Iran now appeared less likely. US President Donald Trump also said that Washington had no immediate plans to strike Iran, as per reports. Apart from that, crude shipments through the Strait of Hormuz -- the key waterway for most Gulf oil supplies -- have recovered to close to pre-war levels, albeit at a higher cost. The dollar index -- which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies -- fell 0.06 per cent to 101.41 after a 0.36 per cent decline in the prior session. Domestic equity benchmarks also traded higher, jumping nearly 2 per cent each on strong global cues. BSE Sensex opened at 78,910.94, an increase of over 1,600 points or 2 per cent, while the NSE Nifty 50 began trade at 24,378.05, up 417.45 points or 1.74 per cent. --IANS

article_sentences: The Court observed that the right to speedy trial, being a fundamental right, cannot be subjected to stringent bail conditions.

The Supreme Court's two-judge bench today expressed reservations about another two-judge bench's judgment in Sukhwinder Singh (2026), which held that the right to speedy trial under Article 21 can't override the stringent statutory requirements for granting bail under Section 37 of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1987 (NDPS).

In the verdict pronounced today in Sujit Das v UOI, a bench comprising Justice Ujjal Bhuyan and Justice Atul S Chandurkar expressed that the judgment in State of Punjab v Sukhwinder Singh @ Gora has become "per incuriam" in the light of the 2021 UOI v KA Najeeb judgment, wherein a three-judge bench held that violation of the right to speedy trial is a ground for constitutional Courts to grant bail even under special statutes which provide for stringent bail conditions.
The bench said: "In Sukhwinder Singh alias Gora, this Court observed that the right to speedy trial rooted in Article 21 of the Constitution is undoubtedly a precious constitutional right.

However, the bench proceeded to observe that in matters governed by special enactments such as the NDPS Act, particularly where the recovery is of commercial quantity, the said right under Article 21 must be exercised within the framework of Section 37 and cannot be pressed into service only on the ground of delay to override Section 37."

Noting this, Justice Bhuyan, who read the pronouncement, stated that while the coordinate bench comprising Justice Sanjay Karol and Justice AG Masih stated that Article 21 and Section 37 of the NDPS Act are to be read harmoniously and not placed in opposition to each other, the present bench feels that when the former is violated, the rigours of special enactments will melt down as held in Najeeb.
He said: "We have our reservations on the aforesaid observations made by the bench.
First and foremost, the rights conferred by Article 21 of the Constitution are not only constitutional rights, these are fundamental rights.
The right to life and liberty as enshrined in Article 21 are at the core of our constitutional jurisprudence.
These fundamental rights cannot be tinkered with so lightly, not even under a special statute."

Further, the bench stated that the observations in Sukhwinder run counter to numerous judgments where it has been reiterated that when there is a violation of Article 21 of the Constitution, the rigour of Section 37 of the NDPS Act or similar provisions under a special statute would have to give way.

Referring to those judgments, the bench said: "Please see Union of India versus K A Najeeb, Satender Kumar Antil, Mohd Muslim, Ankur Chadda, Vijay Singh versus Union of India, where this Court clearly held that Article 21 of the Constitution of India overrides Section 37 of the NDPS Act.

stories.headline: Cabinet Approves Rs.2,814 Crore Critical Mineral Processing Scheme Till 2031
stories.title: Cabinet Approves Rs.2,814 Crore Critical Mineral Processing Scheme Till 2031
stories.summary: The Union Cabinet has approved a Rs.2,814 crore capital expenditure support scheme to establish four domestic critical mineral processing plants, targeting lithium and nickel processing, over FY 2026-27 to FY 2030-31. Under the scheme, the government will provide a capital subsidy of 30% of eligible investment for setting up two lithium processing plants and two nickel processing plants. Each lithium plant must have a minimum processing capacity of 30,000 tonnes (30 kt), while each nickel plant must have a minimum capacity of 50,000 tonnes (50 kt). The maximum capital support has been capped at Rs.500 crore per lithium plant beneficiary and Rs.900 crore per nickel plant beneficiary. The scheme aims to expand India's domestic capacity to process lithium and nickel ores and intermediary products into high-purity compounds. It also provides for the recovery of cobalt as a by-product of nickel processing. Selection and Disbursement of Incentives Beneficiaries will be selected through a two-stage process. Applicants will first undergo technical evaluation, with only qualified applicants eligible to participate in financial bidding. Two beneficiaries will be selected for each mineral based on the least-cost criterion, which means preference will be given to bidders seeking the lowest capital expenditure support from the government. The capital subsidy will be disbursed in three tranches, linked to the achievement of specified project milestones. Reducing Dependence on Critical Mineral Imports India currently depends substantially on imports for refined intermediates and high-purity critical mineral materials, including lithium, nickel and cobalt. Domestic processing capacity remains limited due to high capital requirements, technology constraints and restricted access to raw materials. The new scheme is intended to address these gaps by supporting domestic processing infrastructure and increasing value addition within the country. The proposed capacity is expected to support downstream sectors, including electric mobility, battery energy storage systems (BESS), electronics, defence and speciality steel, where lithium, nickel and cobalt are important raw materials. The scheme will run for five years, from FY 2026-27 to FY 2030-31, with a total financial outlay of Rs.2,814 crore. Key Challenges that could Test India's Critical Mineral Processing Push Raw material availability: While the scheme aims to strengthen domestic processing, securing a consistent supply of lithium and nickel ores will remain a major challenge. Continued reliance on imported feedstock could limit the extent of import substitution. High capital and operating costs: Despite the 30% capital subsidy, high initial investment, energy costs and specialised equipment requirements could affect project viability. Global price volatility: Fluctuations in international lithium and nickel prices could affect raw material procurement costs and the profitability of domestic processing facilities. Demand and offtake challenges: The commercial viability of the proposed plants will also depend on consistent demand from battery manufacturers, electric mobility companies and other downstream industries.

The maximum capital support has been capped at Rs.500 crore per lithium plant beneficiary and Rs.900 crore per nickel plant beneficiary.
The scheme aims to expand India's domestic capacity to process lithium and nickel ores and intermediary products into high-purity compounds.
It also provides for the recovery of cobalt as a by-product of nickel processing.
Selection and Disbursement of Incentives Beneficiaries will be selected through a two-stage process.
Applicants will first undergo technical evaluation, with only qualified applicants eligible to participate in financial bidding.

Two beneficiaries will be selected for each mineral based on the least-cost criterion, which means preference will be given to bidders seeking the lowest capital expenditure support from the government.
The capital subsidy will be disbursed in three tranches, linked to the achievement of specified project milestones.

Reducing Dependence on Critical Mineral Imports India currently depends substantially on imports for refined intermediates and high-purity critical mineral materials, including lithium, nickel and cobalt.
Domestic processing capacity remains limited due to high capital requirements, technology constraints and restricted access to raw materials.
The new scheme is intended to address these gaps by supporting domestic processing infrastructure and increasing value addition within the country.
The scheme will run for five years, from FY 2026-27 to FY 2030-31, with a total financial outlay of Rs.2,814 crore.

Key Challenges that could Test India's Critical Mineral Processing Push Raw material availability: While the scheme aims to strengthen domestic processing, securing a consistent supply of lithium and nickel ores will remain a major challenge.
Continued reliance on imported feedstock could limit the extent of import substitution.
High capital and operating costs: Despite the 30% capital subsidy, high initial investment, energy costs and specialised equipment requirements could affect project viability.
Global price volatility: Fluctuations in international lithium and nickel prices could affect raw material procurement costs and the profitability of domestic processing facilities.

Demand and offtake challenges: The commercial viability of the proposed plants will also depend on consistent demand from battery manufacturers, electric mobility companies and other downstream industries.

stories.title: TN CM Joseph Vijay Writes To PM Narendra Modi Seeking Supreme Court's Regional Bench In Chennai
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: Tamil Nadu Chief Minister Joseph Vijay has written to the Prime Minister of India, Narendra Modi, reiterating the need for setting up a regional bench of the Supreme Court of India in Chennai.
In his letter, Vijay states that when the Constitution was enacted, the framers of the Constitution wanted every citizen of the country to have access to justice.

He added that presently, the remedy under Article 32 of the Constitution was available only to citizens who were geographically closer to the Supreme Court or those who were financially privileged to meet the cost of travel and litigation.

"In this connection, I would like to add that when the constitution was enacted, the framers of the constitution contemplated that all citizens of this country, rich or poor must have direct access to the Court.
It was the main reason for enactment of Article 32, a privilege not available in many other countries.

However, over the time, the remedy under Article 32 is practically available only to citizens who are geographically close to the Supreme Court of India and who are financially privileged to meet the cost of litigation and travel.
However, citizens located mainly in the South India is deprived of availing this remedy due to the sheer distance between the Southern States and New Delhi," the letter states.

Vijay pointed out that as per Article 130 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court shall sit in Delhi, or in such place of places as the Chief Justice of India may, with the approval of the President, from time to time, decide.

He pointed out that setting up of a bench of Supreme Court in Chennai, an important place in South India would benefit all the southern states, as a litigant from south will not have to travel all the way to New Delhi to get their grievance redressed.

He added that establishment of a bench at Chennai would reflect true federal character of the Nation and will not affect the independence of the judiciary since the control over the bench would remain with the Chief Justice of India.

He also stated that the Madras High Court, one of the oldest chartered High Courts in India, had a highly professional, talented, and competent bar which would meet the proposed need of the Supreme Court bench at Chennai.

He further added that despite the State's assurance that it would provide the necessary infrastructure facilities, including residential accommodation for the Supreme Court Judges befitting their status, etc., the full court of the Supreme Court, in its meeting on August 7, 2007, had refused to reconsider its earlier decision against setting up a bench.
